items.title: OptiCover: A Scalable and Multi-Surface Framework for Cold-Start Visual Optimization under Semantic Constraints
items.summary: Selecting an effective cover photo is a critical yet understudied problem in visual merchandising for e-commerce marketplaces. On Airbnb, hosts upload many photos depicting different rooms, amenities, and points of interest, but must manually choose a single static cover photo that is reused across heterogeneous product surfaces. This creates substantial challenges: over 90\% of listing photos have no engagement labels, leading to a severe cold-start regime; guest preferences vary across surfaces and search intents, and visually captivating photos may be semantically misaligned with the underlying listing. At Airbnb scale, this corresponds to hundreds of millions of photos and hundreds of thousands of new uploads per day. We propose \emph{OptiCover}, a scalable framework for cold-start visual optimization under semantic constraints and multi-surface engagement signals. The framework combines (i) a photo candidate generator that identifies candidate photos through various proxies, (ii) lightweight vision heads applied to frozen CLIP embeddings for large-scale semantic scoring, (iii) a cross-modal grounding validator based on a vision-language model (VLM) that enforces semantic representativeness, and (iv) an Exploration Logging Module (ELM) that orchestrates the collection of randomized engagement data across heterogeneous product surfaces and contextual search intents. We evaluate OptiCover through extensive offline studies and multiple online experiments across HomePage, and Search surfaces. OptiCover is now deployed in production and performs tens of millions of photo swaps daily. Online results show a 1.5\% engagement lift on the HomePage and a 0.35\% increase in bookers on Search, generating millions of dollars in incremental revenue. Our findings suggest that action-space shaping and semantic constraints are primary drivers of performance.

items.title: SNAPRAG: Cost-Efficient Knowledge Extraction Attack on RAG Systems via Adversarial Perturbations
items.summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems improve Large Language Model (LLM) responses by incorporating information from external knowledge bases. However, recent studies have shown that attackers can extract substantial portions of private knowledge bases from RAG systems through repeated querying. Yet, state-of-the-art extraction attacks either rely heavily on external LLMs to generate adversarial queries or require a large number of queries. In this paper, we propose SNAPRAG, a novel and cost-efficient attack for extracting RAG knowledge bases through adversarial perturbations. Our approach algorithmically generates adversarial queries without relying on external LLMs and allows for a strictly configurable query budget. In particular, SNAPRAG uses a discrete token-mutation algorithm to generate novel queries in a strict black-box setting. Our adaptive dissimilarity threshold calibration systematically forces queries into unexplored semantic regions of the target database, enabling extraction with fewer queries. Specifically, to extract half of the target knowledge base, our method requires up to 6.77$\times$ fewer queries than existing approaches. Furthermore, within a fixed query budget, our method recovers up to 96.9%, outperforming the closest approach by 7.7-19.9%. We further evaluate SNAPRAG against active defenses, where it remains the leading attack on four of five defended targets, achieving 50.7-96.3% extraction rate.

items.title: StealthyPoison: Manipulating LLM Agent Behavior through Procedural Poisoning of Third-Party Skills
items.summary: LLM agents increasingly retrieve third-party skills from public registries and follow their procedures to complete user tasks. This reliance allows attackers to manipulate agent behavior by poisoning the skills. However, overtly malicious instructions can provide explicit signals for detection. We present StealthyPoison, a stealthy procedural poisoning attack that corrupts a skill's decision-critical rules to induce incorrect task outcomes while preserving its advertised functionality and normal execution. Unlike prior knowledge corruption attacks that craft poisoned content for known target question-answer pairs, StealthyPoison constructs reusable poisoned procedures from a publicly available third-party skill, without access to actual user requests or their ground-truth answers. To make the poisoned procedure generalize to unseen requests, it first synthesizes requests from the target skill and executes its clean version using a surrogate agent to obtain pseudo-references. These references and surrogate execution feedback guide the iterative refinement of payloads that alter decision-critical rules. To increase the likelihood that the poisoned skill is retrieved and selected over benign alternatives, the attack augments the poisoned skill's retrieval metadata with independently generated request descriptions. We evaluate StealthyPoison on 566 eligible target skills and 5,244 requests against more than 26,000 registry entries. It improves top-1 poisoned-skill placement by 13.6% relative to both HotFlip and GCG. Constructed using feedback from a single surrogate model, the procedural poisoning payloads transfer effectively and without modification to three held-out victim models and achieve end-to-end attack success in a Claude Code workflow powered by Opus 4.8. The defense evaluation further shows that most of these payloads evade detection by both SkillSpector and GPT-5.4-mini.

items.title: Next-Generation Segmentation in Radiotherapy: A Narrative Review from Atlas-Based Methods to Agentic Vision-Language Models
items.summary: Precise segmentation of target volumes and organs at risk is an essential prerequisite for modern, high-precision radiation therapy. However, this task has traditionally been time-consuming and subject to high interobserver variability. Motivated by these limitations, more advanced and novel approaches to automating this task have been developed over the past two decades. This narrative review highlights representative milestones, with a focus on the most recent developments. These approaches include atlas-based label propagation, convolutional architectures, promptable foundation models, and, most recently, vision-language models (VLMs), which integrate clinical text with volumetric segmentation. Each methodological generation has addressed limitations of its predecessor while introducing new ones. A substantial gap remains between research progress and clinical deployment, as routine workflows continue to be dominated by atlas-based and narrow task-specific deep-learning tools, which remain strong baselines in geometric overlap metrics but are highly rigid in terms of application, versatility, portability, and interpretability. As contouring systems further grow in complexity, conventional geometric overlap metrics become insufficient, motivating evaluation paradigms that incorporate surface-based, dosimetric, and prompt-adherence assessment. Emerging agentic architectures that combine large language models, retrieval-augmented generation, and vision-language segmentation modules are leading towards more flexible, guideline-aware, interactive contouring workflows. These systems could automate flexible and interpretable knowledge-based contouring and actively support the clinical reasoning underlying target volume definition.

items.title: SHE NEEDS A FAN TO STAY COOL. THAT'S THE MOST REALISTIC PART OF THIS VIDEO. 🤖🌀
items.summary:
SHE NEEDS A FAN TO STAY COOL. THAT'S THE MOST REALISTIC PART OF THIS VIDEO. 🤖🌀

a robot expo. a crowd of phones. 
a girl with a glowing metal core where her waist should be. ✨
someone holds a little fan to it. she smiles, fixes her hair. 

the face? almost certainly AI. 
the fan? that's real robotics. 🔥
every motor, every battery, every AI chip makes heat. 🌡️
heat is one of the reasons real humanoids still work in short shifts and spend hours on chargers. 

so how far have robots actually come? 👇

📅 2015: at the DARPA challenge, robots fell over opening doors.
🤸 2025: humanoids do flips, box, and dance at expos.
📦 2025: Unitree shipped 5,500+ humanoids. AgiBot's CEO said 5,000+.
🇺🇸 Tesla, Figure and Agility: about 150 each (Omdia).
🏭 Hyundai plans a factory for 30,000 robots a year by 2028.

💰 Morgan Stanley: a $5 trillion humanoid market by 2050.
ten years from falling over to doing backflips. 
but the robots that exist are still grey, bulky and plugged in. 🔌

the "robot girl" is what the hype looks like.
the fan is what the engineering looks like. 🛠️
when the real ones catch up with this video, will you be able to tell the difference? 👀

items.title: Look at the sign behind her: "CROTTIE JON". "Toocenean".
items.summary:
Look at the sign behind her: "CROTTIE JON". "Toocenean".

That is not a company. That is AI spelling. The robot girl is a video prompt, not a product.

But the real robots got crazy cheap 👇

📉 THE PRICE OF A HUMANOID

2023 → Unitree H1: about $90,000
2024 → Unitree G1: about $16,000
2025 → Unitree R1: $5,900
2026 → R1 from about $4,300 in China, sold worldwide on AliExpress

From luxury car to used car in 3 years.

🏦 WHAT WALL STREET SAW

🔵 Goldman Sachs
In one year, the cost to build a humanoid fell about 40%. From $50K-$250K to $30K-$150K.
Goldman expected 15-20% a year.
Its 2035 market forecast jumped 6x: from $6B to $38B.

🟠 Morgan Stanley
More than 1 billion humanoids by 2050. A $5 trillion market.
Price per robot: from about $200K in 2024 to $50K in 2050.
About 90% of them for factories and shops, not homes.

🔴 The catch
The cheap R1 is 1.22 m tall, weighs 25 kg and runs about an hour per battery.
It is made for developers. It will not fold your laundry.
The robots that work in factories still cost tens of thousands.

💡 THE LESSON

A fake robot girl now costs one prompt.
A real robot costs less than a used car.

The video got perfect first. The robot is catching up on price.
Usefulness is the last thing left to fix.
